messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai had always been a man who liked his routine. As an electrician, he took pride in being on time and getting the job done efficiently. But all of that changed on a fateful evening two years ago when he was assaulted by a group of strangers while walking home from work. The event occurred at exactly 8:45 PM, and ever since then, Kai had found himself growing increasingly anxious as the clock approached that time every day. As the anniversary of the assault drew near, Kai began to feel detached and unreal, like he was observing his life from outside his body. He would catch himself zoning out in the middle of conversations or staring blankly at walls for minutes on end. It was as if his mind had developed a coping mechanism to deal with the trauma, but it only seemed to make things worse. To avoid these feelings, Kai started spending more and more time on his phone, playing games or scrolling through social media until the early hours of the morning. But even that couldn't block out the triggers that haunted him. Every time he heard a door slam shut or saw someone approaching him unexpectedly, Kai's heart would skip a beat. He would react with alarm, his senses on high alert as if he was still in danger. His partner had started to notice these episodes and tried to reassure him, but Kai couldn't shake off the feeling that he was constantly being watched. When memories of the assault flooded back, Kai felt like he was reliving it all over again. He remembered the sound of footsteps behind him, the feeling of fear as he realized he was being attacked. But there were gaps in his memory too - moments where everything went black and he couldn't recall what happened next. This incomplete picture only fueled his guilt and self-blame. Kai had come to believe that if only he had been more aware of his surroundings or reacted faster, the assault might not have happened. As these thoughts swirled in his head, Kai started to question his own character. He wondered if there was something fundamentally flawed about him that made him a target for violence. This sense of hopelessness crept into every aspect of his life, making him doubt his future and compare himself unfavorably to others. Why had he been so foolish as to walk alone at night? Why hadn't he fought back harder? Kai's negative appraisals fed back into his threat perception, making him even more vigilant and jumpy. He began avoiding unfamiliar places or situations where he might feel vulnerable, always scanning the surroundings for potential dangers. This hypervigilance only seemed to heighten his sense of anxiety, creating a vicious cycle that left Kai exhausted and drained. As the months went by, Kai's substance use increased too - a few drinks after work to calm his nerves or medication to help him sleep. He knew it wasn't healthy, but he felt like he had no other way to cope with the memories and emotions that haunted him. His partner tried to stage an intervention, but Kai pushed them away, convinced that they just didn't understand what he was going through. It was only when Kai's job began to suffer - missed deadlines, botched repairs - that he realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living in this state of constant fear and self-doubt. As he sat in the therapist's office for the first time, Kai felt a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, he could break free from this cycle of trauma and start rebuilding his life. But as he looked back on the past two years, Kai couldn't shake off the fear that had taken hold of him. What if he never regained control over his memories? What if the triggers always stayed one step ahead of him? The uncertainty was suffocating, but for now, it was all Kai could do to take a tentative step forward and hope that someday, somehow, things would get better.
